title: The wrong bishop
summary: Recognise the wrong bishop, bring the king to the corner to draw and, from the other side, shut the corner door to win.
part.corner.title: The wrong bishop
part.corner.summary: With the wrong bishop, the king in the corner draws; with the right bishop, one check drives it out.
part.cutoff.title: Shutting the corner
part.cutoff.summary: The attacker keeps the king out of the corner: the bishop covers g8 and, when the king comes down the h-file, the king itself shuts the door.
part.race.title: The race to the corner
part.race.summary: Standing in front of the pawn is not enough. The king must get into the corner, and every move counts.
part.sacrifice.title: Fischer–Taimanov
part.sacrifice.summary: Against Fischer, Taimanov could have given up the knight and run to the corner, and he missed it.
part.transform.title: From g-pawn to h-pawn
part.transform.summary: A piece given up makes the g-pawn capture and become an h-pawn, and the bishop turns into the wrong one. Greco, Kasparov and a knight that gives itself up.
part.shift.title: Changing the file
part.shift.summary: With a rook pawn and a neighbour, make the neighbour disappear, and do not let your rook pawn become the pawn on the other file.
part.prison.title: The corner as a prison
part.prison.summary: With a g-pawn next to the h-pawn, the king shut in on h8 lets the pawn through.
part.summary.title: Summary
part.summary.summary: Three rules and one race played to the end.
step.t_corner: A bishop and a pawn up, and the black king is already on h8. Before any calculation, look at the colour of the corner and the colour of the bishop. Can White win?
step.t_corner.hint1: For the pawn to queen, the black king has to leave h8. Who can force it to?
step.t_corner.hint2: h8 is a dark square. The bishop on f1 only moves on light ones.
step.corner: This is the wrong bishop. The h-pawn queens on h8, a dark square, and White's bishop lives on the light squares. It can never check on h8, never cover h8. The black king stays there, steps to g8 or h7 and back, and nothing drives it out. With a whole piece more, White can only stalemate.
step.d_corner: I will play White and try everything. Watch what happens to the black king.
step.d_corner.m1: 1.h6. The pawn advances and takes g7 away from the black king.
step.d_corner.m2: 1...Kg8. No hurry: the king swings between h8 and g8. A check on g8 only sends it back to h8.
step.d_corner.m3: 2.Kg6. Now g7 and h7 are closed.
step.d_corner.m4: 2...Kh8, the only drawing move, and the only one it needs. Had it gone to f8, 3.h7 would follow and the pawn would queen: the black king would never reach the corner again.
step.d_corner.m5: 3.h7, and Black has no move: g8 is covered by the pawn, g7 by the king. Stalemate. A draw.
step.colour: Now I change one thing only: the bishop is on e1, on the dark squares. h8 is dark, and this bishop checks in the corner. The rule: look at the rook pawn's promotion square. If the bishop does not move on it, the king in the corner draws. On the a-file it is the mirror: a8 is light, and the wrong bishop for the a-pawn is the dark-squared one.
step.d_right: With the right bishop, the black king in the corner does not hold. Watch.
step.d_right.m1: 1.Kg6. The white king covers g7 and h7.
step.d_right.m2: 1...Kg8, the only move: g7 and h7 belong to the white king.
step.d_right.m3: 2.h6. No hurry: the pawn comes closer.
step.d_right.m4: 2...Kh8. The king goes back to the corner; against the light-squared bishop, that would be enough.
step.d_right.m5: 3.Bc3+ is the check the wrong bishop could never give.
step.d_right.m6: 3...Kg8. The king is forced out: the corner is in check.
step.d_right.m7: 4.h7+ pushes the king away. It only has f8, because g7 belongs to the white king and h8 to the bishop, and 5.h8=Q+ queens. The right bishop made all the difference.
step.rightMove: Now the bishop is the right one, and White wins. But careful: one natural move here throws it all away.
step.rightMove.done: Well done. Bishop check, the pawn pushes the king away and queens. 1.h7 on the first move would have been stalemate.
step.rightMove.hint: 1.h7 now stalemates the black king. First get the king out of the corner with the bishop.
step.t_cutoff: The bishop is the wrong one again, but the black king is still on f8, outside the corner. How do you stop it from reaching h8?
step.t_cutoff.hint1: Through which square does the black king want to enter the corner?
step.t_cutoff.hint2: g8 is light. White's bishop can cover it.
step.cutoff: If the king gets into the corner, it is a draw. So White's job is to shut the door first. The black king's way in is through g8; g8 is a light square, and the bishop can cover it: 1.Bc4! (1.Kh7 also works). The white king looks after g7 and h7. With the doors shut, the black king stays outside and the pawn walks up.
step.d_cutoff: Watch White shut the door and then bring the pawn home.
step.d_cutoff.m1: 1.Bc4! The bishop covers g8, the door to the corner.
step.d_cutoff.m2: 1...Ke7. g8 belongs to the bishop, g7 and f7 to the white king: the black king cannot get in and backs away.
step.d_cutoff.m3: 2.Kg7. The white king settles next to the corner.
step.d_cutoff.m4: 2...Kd6. With no way into the corner, the black king tries to hunt the pawn through the centre.
step.d_cutoff.m5: 3.h6. The pawn runs with the king guarding its path and queens in two moves. The door stayed shut the whole time.
step.kingDoor: Sometimes the black king does not come in through g8 but down the h-file. This is a position by Edmar Mednis: the black king is on h6 and wants h7 and h8. The bishop on f7 already covers g8, and that is not enough. The king shuts the door: 1.Kg8! covers h7 and h8 at once (1.Bg6, closing h7, also wins).
step.d_kingDoor: White shuts the door with the king, and the pawn goes through.
step.d_kingDoor.m1: 1.Kg8! Now h7 and h8 belong to the white king.
step.d_kingDoor.m2: 1...Kg5, the only move: h7 and g7 belong to the white king, and g6 to the pawn.
step.d_kingDoor.m3: 2.Kg7. The king stays next to the corner and escorts the pawn. The h5-pawn is protected by the bishop, and the black king cannot come back: the pawn queens.
step.kingDoorMove: The black king is next to h7 and wants to get into the corner. Who shuts the door?
step.kingDoorMove.done: That's it. 1.Kg8! shuts h7, h8 and g7. After 1.h5+? Kh7! or 1.Bd3+? Kh6, the black king would come down the h-file and draw.
step.kingDoorMove.hint: A check from the bishop or the pawn does not shut the door. Which piece covers h7, h8 and g7 at the same time?
step.t_mednis: Mednis's position again, now with Black to move. Your king is in front of the pawn, on h6. Is that enough, or does it need to be somewhere else?
step.t_mednis.hint1: If the white king reaches g8 or g7, what happens to your king?
step.t_mednis.hint2: In front of the pawn is not the same as inside the corner.
step.mednis: In the previous chapter, with White to move, 1.Kg8! won. Now Black moves first. In the king and rook pawn against king ending, standing in front of the pawn is enough. With the bishop it is not: the king must get into the corner before the white king shuts the door. 1...Kh7! and then 2...Kh8.
step.d_mednis: I will defend with Black. First I get into the corner, then I simply stay.
step.d_mednis.m1: 1...Kh7! From here the king steps onto h8 next move; g8 belongs to the bishop, but I do not need it.
step.d_mednis.m2: 2.Ke7. The white king cannot go to g8, next to my king, and goes round to reach g7.
step.d_mednis.m4: 3.Kf6. Now g7 is within its reach, but I am already inside.
step.d_mednis.m5: 3...Kh7, and nobody gets me out of here. A draw.
step.tempo: Now a real race. Count your king's moves to the corner and the white king's moves to g7. Pick the square that covers the ways into the corner, even if the bishop threatens to shut one of them. And when you also have a pawn, threatening to queen it gains time: every move the other side spends stopping it is one more move for your king. That is the idea of Réti's manoeuvre.
step.raceMove: The white king and bishop want to shut the corner. Run to h8 without wasting time.
step.raceMove.done: That's it. You went along the diagonal and, when the bishop came to c2, 4...Kg7 was the only move. Now the king is home.
step.raceMove.hint: Head for g7 along the diagonal. Once the bishop covers h7, the only door left is g7.
step.t_taimanov: Vancouver, 1971, the Candidates, the series of matches that picks the world champion's challenger. Bobby Fischer, with White, faces Mark Taimanov in game 2. After 80...Rxf6+ 81.Kxf6, Black was left with a knight against bishop and h-pawn, and the black king far from h8. Look at the colour of h8 and the colour of the white bishop. Which plan saves Black?
step.t_taimanov.hint1: Think about what happens if the knight disappears from the board. Which ending is left?
step.t_taimanov.hint2: Light-squared bishop and h-pawn: the wrong bishop. The knight can offer itself.
step.taimanov: Black does not need the knight. If it leaves the board, what remains is the light-squared bishop and the h-pawn: the wrong bishop. The knight goes to d3 and f4, watches the pawn and offers itself; while White spends moves on it, the black king runs to h8. Taimanov played 81...Ke4?? and took his king away from the corner. He lost.
step.d_taimanov: The plan that would have saved Taimanov.
step.d_taimanov.m1: 81...Nd3! The knight heads for f4, where it covers h5 and h3.
step.d_taimanov.m2: 82.h4. The pawn tries to run before the knight reaches f4 to watch it.
step.d_taimanov.m3: 82...Nf4, the only move: the knight covers h5 and stops the pawn.
step.d_taimanov.m5: 83...Kd6! I do not defend the knight: I run to the corner.
step.d_taimanov.m6: 84.Kxf4. The knight has left the board, and the wrong bishop is what remains.
step.d_taimanov.m7: 84...Ke7, the only move, and the king reaches f8 and g8 in time. A draw.
step.taimanovGame: In the game, after 81...Ke4??, Fischer played 82.Bc8! and took f5 away from the black king; then 83.h4 and 84.h5 were each the only winning move. The knight alone could not hold the rook pawn. After 89.Kf6, Taimanov resigned, and Fischer won the match 6-0.
step.taimanovMove: Now play Taimanov's side with the plan that would have saved him.
step.taimanovMove.done: That's it. 83...Ke5 defends the knight and keeps the king on its way to the corner. 83...Kd6, which drops the knight and runs to e7, also holds, as in the demonstration.
step.taimanovMove.hint: First the knight watches the pawn; when it is attacked, your king goes towards the corner, not away from it.
step.t_greco: A study by the Italian Gioachino Greco, from 1623, just after the rooks have been traded. White has g- and h-pawns and the light-squared bishop. For that bishop, the h-pawn is the wrong pawn; the g-pawn is not. How does Black make the g-pawn leave the g-file?
step.t_greco.hint1: On which square does each pawn queen, and what colour is it?
step.t_greco.hint2: If the g-pawn captures something, which file does it go to?
step.greco: 1...Bh3! offers the bishop. If 2.gxh3, the g-pawn becomes a second h-pawn: two h-pawns and the light-squared bishop, the wrong bishop. If White does not capture, Black's bishop captures the g-pawn and a lone h-pawn is left. Two rook pawns on the same file are worth no more than one.
step.d_greco: I will play Black. First the bishop offers itself, then the king runs to the corner.
step.d_greco.m1: 1...Bh3! The bishop offers itself to the g-pawn.
step.d_greco.m2: 2.gxh3. The g-pawn has become an h-pawn: now there are two h-pawns, and h8 is dark.
step.d_greco.m3: 2...Kh6. The king heads straight for h7 and h8. The pawns are far from queening, and White's bishop will never cover h8. A draw.
step.karpovKasparov: Moscow, 1985, game 20 of the world championship match. Garry Kasparov, with Black, was defending a bishop ending against the champion, Anatoly Karpov. He gave two pawns for one: 82...Bb3! 83.Be8 Ke7 84.Bxg6 Bxa4 85.Bxf5 Kf6. White was left with f- and h-pawns; the black bishop gives itself up for the f-pawn when needed, and what remains is the h-pawn with the light-squared bishop, which does not cover h8. A draw was agreed, and Kasparov went on to win the match and become world champion.
step.quizKnight: Black has g- and h-pawns and the dark-squared bishop; h1 is light.
step.quizKnight.done: That's it. 1.Ne5+! and 2.Nxg6! The knight is lost, but it captures the g-pawn with it, and the white king goes to h1.
step.quizKnight.hint: Without the g-pawn, the remaining pawn is a rook pawn, and Black's bishop does not move on h1. A check gives the knight the time it needs.
step.t_shift: Black has a- and b-pawns and the light-squared bishop. The a-pawn alone, with that bishop, would be the wrong pawn: a1 is dark. How do you make the b-pawn disappear?
step.t_shift.hint1: If the b-pawn captures, it goes to the a-file; if the king captures, the b-pawn disappears.
step.t_shift.hint2: The b-pawn and the black king are on the same diagonal. Which white piece can use that?
step.shift: 1.Ba4! pins the b-pawn to the king. If 1...bxa4, the b-pawn becomes a second a-pawn: two a-pawns and the light-squared bishop, and the white king heads for b1 and a1. If the king steps out of the pin, 2.Bxb5 and the b-pawn disappears just the same.
step.d_shift: First the line where the pawn captures the bishop.
step.d_shift.m1: 1.Ba4! The bishop offers itself and pins the b-pawn.
step.d_shift.m2: 1...bxa4. The b-pawn has gone to the a-file: now there are two a-pawns.
step.d_shift.m3: 2.Kc2. The white king runs to b1 and a1.
step.d_shift.m4: 2...a3. The pawn advances, but a1 is dark and Black's bishop never covers it.
step.d_shift.m5: 3.Kb1, and the king reaches the corner. A draw.
step.shiftWrong: Now the other side of the coin, in a neighbouring position: Black also has a pawn on a6. After 1.Ba4 Kc5 2.Bxb5, Black does not recapture with the king. 2...axb5! The a-pawn becomes a b-pawn, and b1 is light: now Black's bishop is the right one and Black wins. With 2...Kxb5? only the a-pawn would be left, and it was a draw. The defender does the same sum: do not let an opponent's rook pawn capture and change file.
step.shiftMove.done: That's it. 1.Ba4! and 2.Bxb5! The a-pawn is left with the light-squared bishop, and your king goes to a1.
step.shiftMove.hint: First pin the pawn; if the king steps out of the pin, give the bishop for the b-pawn.
step.t_prison: Opposite-coloured bishops. For White's light-squared bishop, the h-pawn is the wrong pawn, and the black king is already on h8. But there is a g-pawn next to it. Can White win?
step.t_prison.hint1: Count the black king's squares: h7, g7 and g8. Who covers each one?
step.t_prison.hint2: h7 and g7 already belong to the pawns. One light square is missing.
step.prison: 1.Bc4! covers g8, and the black king has no square: h7 belongs to the g-pawn, g7 to the h-pawn. It is shut in, and only the black bishop can move. The white king walks to f7, and the g-pawn advances with check. With a single rook pawn, the corner saves; with the g-pawn next to it, the corner is a trap.
step.d_prison.m1: 1.Bc4! The black king has no move left; only the bishop can move.
step.d_prison.m2: 1...Bc3. Black can only pass with the bishop.
step.d_prison.m3: 2.Kf5. The white king heads for f7, in no hurry: the black king cannot get out.
step.d_prison.m4: 2...Bb2. The bishop stays on the long diagonal, eyeing g7.
step.d_prison.m7: 4.Kf7. Now the king covers g7 and g8, and 5.g7+! comes with check. After 5...Bxg7 and 6.hxg7+ the new g-pawn queens on g8 with the king's support.
step.prisonMove.done: That's it. 1.Bc4! The bishop shuts g8, and the white king walks to f7.
step.prisonMove.hint: Which light square does the black king still have?
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. First: look at the colour of the rook pawn's promotion square. If the bishop does not move on it, the king in the corner draws, and two rook pawns on the same file do not change that.
step.rules: Second: the attacker shuts the door first, with the bishop covering g8 or with the king on g8 and g7. The defender gets into the corner, not just in front of the pawn, and gives up a piece if needed to get there.
step.rules3: Third: a capture changes the file. Give up a piece so that the neighbouring pawn disappears or becomes a rook pawn; do not let the opponent's rook pawn capture and change file; and, if the other pawn is not a rook pawn, the corner can become a prison. Now play a race to the end.
step.finish: Take the king to h8 without wasting time.
ex.e09: Each side has a bishop, of opposite colours, and White has two pawns. Beware of the natural move. Find the draw.
ex.e09.hint: The corner looks safe, but the g-pawn is not a rook pawn. Keep your king watching f7 and g7.
ex.e09.solution: 1...Kf8! 1...Kh8?? loses: 2.Ke6 Kg8 3.Ke7+ Kh8 4.Kf7 and the g-pawn goes through. With the king on f8, the white king cannot reach f7.
key.corner: The black king in the corner, a rook pawn and a bishop that can't reach the promotion square: a draw, whoever moves. The black king never leaves.
key.rightBishop: The same position, but with the bishop of the corner's colour: now it drives the black king out, and White wins.
key.aPawn: The same draw on the other side of the board: with the a-pawn, the wrong bishop is the dark-squared one.
key.cutoff: The black king hasn't reached the corner yet: the bishop hurries to shut the door before it gets in, and White wins.
key.mednis: Being near the corner isn't enough: the black king has to get into it. The move decides: if White is to move, White wins; if Black is to move, it's a draw.
key.fischerTaimanov: Fischer against Taimanov, Vancouver, 1971: by giving up the knight, Taimanov would have reached the wrong-bishop draw. He missed it and lost.
history: An extra bishop and pawn should win, right? Not always. If the pawn is a rook pawn, on the edge file, and the bishop doesn't travel on the colour of the corner where the pawn promotes, the defending king only has to reach that corner: nobody can drive it out, and it's a draw. This is the wrong bishop, one of the most important surprises in endgames, because it works both ways: the side that is worse off can save itself with it. The idea is old: it already appears in a study by the Italian Gioachino Greco, from the seventeenth century. And great players have won and lost because of it: in Vancouver, in 1971, Mark Taimanov could have given up his knight and run to the corner against Bobby Fischer, saving the draw, but he missed it and lost.
practice: Now the practical challenge, with White: shut the door and bring the pawn all the way.
ex.e12: The black king is already near the corner and the bishop sits on a2. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: a1 is a dark square and Black's bishop is light-squared. Your king needs to reach b1 or a1 before the bishop takes b1.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kc2! The king covers b1, b2 and b3 and stands one step from the corner. After 1...Bb3+ comes 2.Kb1!, and the white king shuttles between b1 and a1: the light-squared bishop never drives it off a1. With 1.Kc3? Bb1! the bishop shuts the door, the black king gets out via b2 and the pawn runs.
ex.e13: The bishop is the wrong one and the black king is running for h8. Which piece shuts the door? Find the winning move.
ex.e13.hint: Covering g8 with the bishop is not enough: the black king can walk down the h-file. What covers h7 and h8 at once?
ex.e13.solution: 1.Kf7! (1.Kf8 also works) and, after 1...Kh6, 2.Kg8! (or 2.Bf5, covering h7): the white king holds h7 and h8 and the pawn walks up. The natural 1.Be6? covers g8, but 1...Kh6 and the black king gets in via the h-file, h7 and h8: draw.
ex.e14: Your b-pawn is a problem: White wants to trade it and get a b-pawn. Where does the king go? Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: If a white a-pawn captures onto b6, the bishop is no longer the wrong one. Do not give White time for a5, and do not push your pawn.
ex.e14.solution: 1...Kb8! The king stays one step from a8. If 2.Bxb6, 2...Ka8! and only a-pawns are left with the dark-squared bishop: draw. 1...Ka7? loses to 2.a5! Kxa6 3.axb6, and the b-pawn queens on b8, a dark square. 1...b5? 2.axb5 gives the same b-pawn.
ex.e15: Trading bishops looks safe, but the pawn ending is lost. There is another way. Find the draw.
ex.e15.hint: If Black's b-pawn turns into an a-pawn, what colour is a1? And which squares does Black's bishop move on?
ex.e15.solution: 1.a5! If 1...bxa5, Black's pawn becomes an a-pawn and Black's bishop is light-squared, the wrong one for a1. Then 2.Kf2!, and the king runs to b1 and a1 in time. If 1...Bxh1, 2.axb6 and Black's bishop is tied to b7: with no black pawn left, it is a draw. 1.Bxd5+? Kxd5 loses: the white king cannot catch the pawns.
ex.e16: One pawn against bishop and pawn. Three only moves in a row. Find the draw.
ex.e16.hint: h1 is light and Black's bishop is dark-squared. Your king must get to h1, but the a-pawn can win the tempi it needs.
ex.e16.solution: 1.a6! (the pawn steps out of the black king's reach) 1...Bc5 2.Kc7! 2...h5 3.Kc6! The king covers b5 and threatens 4.Kb7 and 5.a7, so the bishop has to watch a7; after 3...Bg1 4.a7 Bxa7 5.Kd5 the white king is inside the h-pawn's square and reaches h1. Every white move was the only one: 2.Kb7?, for example, arrives one tempo late.
ex.e17: Bishop and knight against bishop and two pawns, with the white king already on h1. Find the draw.
ex.e17.hint: With the g-pawn, Black's bishop is the right one for g1. Make the g-pawn capture onto the h-file, and for that your bishop has to reach h6 with tempo.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Nd2!! Kxd2 2.Bg5+! Kd1 3.Bh6!! The knight lures the king to d2 so that 2.Bg5 comes with check and the bishop reaches h6 without losing time. If 3...gxh6, Black is left with two h-pawns and the dark-squared bishop, the wrong one for h1. If the g-pawn advances, 4.Bxf8; if the bishop moves away, 4.Bxg7. Either way the white king holds the corner.
